title: The Real Reason Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond
text:
Picking a new James Bond has long followed a tried-and-tested formula: Don’t go too famous. The secret agent has nearly always been played by an up-and-coming, well-regarded talent who looks good in a tux. So for years, as the debate has dragged on over who would replace Daniel Craig in the role, dozens of names along those lines have bubbled up; these most recently included Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor. Some possible candidates aged out of the role while waiting for it to open up, in the same way that potential popes find themselves hitting retirement age before their chance at the papacy arrives. But the final choice for the new Bond, Robert Pattinson, completely defies that established logic: By casting someone who’s already globally popular, the franchise is somehow taking the risky version of a typically very safe bet.

 Pattinson makes plenty of sense on paper as Bond: He’s about the right age (he turned 40 this year) and the right height, at 6 foot 1; he’s debonair and British in all the appreciable ways; he wears a suit better than anyone. (His work in Tenet is one of the best-tailored performances of all time.) But unlike most of his predecessors, he’s also one of the most famous A-listers working today. He’s featured in multiple hit franchises and is also the current occupant of another iconic role, Batman. And because the Bond franchise is in the hands of new ownership for the first time in decades, the old formulas clearly no longer apply.

 Pattinson’s career started out traditionally enough. He first broke out as a teenager playing Cedric Diggory in the fourth Harry Potter movie before becoming a superstar in his 20s thanks to the Twilight movies—dark romantic fantasies aimed at young adults that were largely dismissed or mocked by critics upon release. But the actor has harnessed his early celebrity to create a constantly shifting and unique persona as a performer. He’s worked with numerous acclaimed directors across genres, Christopher Nolan, David Cronenberg, James Gray, Claire Denis, the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers, Bong Joon Ho, and Lynne Ramsay among them. When he’s appeared in more conventional blockbusters, he’s put a weird imprimatur on them, as with his emo version of Batman; in December, he’s popping up in Dune: Part Three as an eyebrow-less, shapeshifting villain.

 [ Read: The James Bond trap ] 

 In a way, playing Bond seems almost too normal for Pattinson. He certainly looks the part in the one promo image that Amazon dropped; he’s a handsome Brit with a chiseled jaw who’s clad in a tux and toting a gun, as per usual for the MI6 super-spy. But one hopes he’ll be able to bring a stranger energy to the role than the Bonds before him. Craig played the character in five movies, culminating in 2021’s No Time to Die ; his take was flinty and frightening, a swerve from Pierce Brosnan’s suave demeanor. Pattinson will likely come across as even more sophisticated—he’s taller and more willowy than Craig, and more traditionally “posh.” And the DC cinematic universe’s recent behind-the-scenes shake-up probably helped Pattinson commit to the franchise, considering that his future as Batman now seems murky. But I hope there’s room in his schedule to maintain the wacky streak he’s shown in movies such as last year’s Mickey 17 , as well as the more alien, lizard-like quality that made his performance in The Batman , along with this year’s The Odyssey and Primetime , so compelling.

 In previous eras, one would be foolish to hope for that sort of originality. The Bond property had long been a rarity in Hollywood: It was essentially run as a tightly controlled family business. Eon Productions, which was led by the producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli, managed the franchise that they’d inherited from their father; creatively, the buck stopped with them. They relied on a core group of collaborators who knew what a Bond movie should look and feel like, extending beyond whoever was playing the role. That consistency was helpful in building the brand, but it sometimes felt stultifying. Now that Amazon owns Bond outright, the company is making choices that suggest that a more prestigious take on the character is en route.

 This is not to diss some of the prior Bond films’ directors. Sam Mendes, who made two of the Craig movies, is an Oscar winner—yet he’d made a few flops before he got the gig. Directors such as Cary Fukunaga, Marc Forster, Martin Campbell, and Lee Tamahori were all fairly reliable picks with some large-canvas action experience. But the next installment’s director, Denis Villeneuve, is a glitzy choice: He’s highly regarded by critics and is coming off a giant franchise success of his own with Dune . Among action filmmakers, only Nolan is a bigger name right now (and he was reportedly counted out for the job because he’d require the right to final cut—i.e., total creative control).

 Amazon’s decision to spare no expense or risk for handling the biggest name-brand property it owns seems obvious. For all the creative ups and downs of the Craig era, the actor was a beloved Bond for 15 years; his memory will be difficult to displace. Rather than roll the dice on a (relative) unknown in search of something new and different, the brand’s new owners are opting for A-list quality. Pattinson is not an outside-the-box choice for Bond. Somehow, he still feels like a total surprise.
